extracted.intended_audience: journalism/media scholars, graduate students, and practitioners (television reporters, news managers) interested in media influence research
extracted.subtask_description: A Web-based survey instrument and accompanying methodological discussion used in a dissertation to measure television reporters' perceptions of multiple sources of influence on news content (advertisers, owners, politicians, public relations, organizational pressures) and to validate an Interorganizational Model of Content (IOMC) via structural equation modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extramedia Influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Forces outside the media (measured by instances of advertiser, public relations, and political/government official pressures) directly affect influences at the Organizational level and ultimately news content and coverage decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study measured extramedia influences via multiple survey items asking how often advertisers, politicians/government officials, and public relations practitioners (including VNRs/prepackaged materials) try to influence which stories are covered, how they are covered (angle/stance), or try to get stories not covered. Examples: items 7–14 (advertisers), 22–34 (politicians/government officials), and 35–44 (public relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational Influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Influences at the organizational level (e.g., station owners and top-level executives, bottom-line pressures) directly influence within-media sources and also show a direct influence on content and coverage decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured by items about owners/top-level executives influencing coverage (items 4, 15–21) and perceptions of profit-over-quality and bottom-line pressures (items 5–6). The validated IOMC model found organizational forces both mediate extramedia influences and sometimes directly affect content without passing through within-media gatekeepers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Within-Media Influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources within the news organization (e.g., newsroom managers) that mediate organizational influences before those influences affect news content and coverage decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within-media influences are conceptualized as the newsroom-level actors/forces measured in the study (implicitly via items and model paths). The model suggests a chain: Extramedia -> Organizational -> Within-Media -> Content, with newsroom managers treated as a source-of-measure at the Within-Media level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influences on News Content and Coverage Decisions (Dependent Variable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters' perceptions of how various forces (extramedia, organizational, within-media) affect news content selection, angle, emphasis, omission, and coverage decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final validated model reportedly explained 90% of the variance in this dependent construct. Measurement is via reporter responses to frequency/agreement items about pressures and content changes (e.g., 'How often do journalists/stations not cover (avoid covering) stories or topics because of influences from ...?').

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda Cutting (definition and indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agenda cutting may occur when an item is (1) placed low on the news agenda (buried); (2) removed from the agenda once it is there; or (3) ignored because it was never put on the news agenda in the first place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agenda cutting is proposed to occur because of logistical constraints, external and internal influences, and/or journalists' own prejudices. The study found agenda cutting most likely due to extramedia and organizational influences, with smaller effects from logistical constraints (e.g., staff-size pressures). Researchers should consider experimental designs to assess audience effects of agenda cutting (present altered media products and test knowledge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Staffing / Logistical Constraints as Influence Factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Inadequate staff size and staff reductions negatively affect the quality of news coverage and may contribute to agenda cutting or reliance on external materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey items include agreement scales: 'An inadequate staff size hurts the quality of news coverage.'; 'When the size of staff is reduced at a station, it has negative effects on news coverage.'; and 'Public relations or advertising materials fill holes in news programs caused by lack of staff.' Use these items to operationalize logistical influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertiser Influence (frequency and mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers can pressure for favorable coverage, influence decisions not to run stories (including threats to pull ads), influence which stories are covered or emphasized, and influence how stories are covered (angle/stance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured by multiple frequency items (almost never to very often): e.g., 'How often do advertisers pressure TV stations/journalists for favorable coverage?' and 'How often do stations/journalists decide not to run some stories because of advertiser pressures?' (items 7–14). Use these items to quantify advertiser-related extramedia pressure and its effects on coverage and framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owners / Top-Level Executive Influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners and top-level executives may influence news coverage by pressuring to avoid stories, shaping emphasis, or setting profit/agenda priorities; perceived frequency measured by reporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey items (4, 15–21) ask about owners' influence on not running stories, emphasizing stories, shaping angles, and trying to influence which stories are covered. Also capture perceptions of owners' profit focus (item 5) and whether station staff are pressured to handle stories involving firms with economic clout (item 47).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political / Government Official Influence (including leaks and VNRs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Politicians or government officials may pressure stations for favorable coverage, provide leaks/off-the-record interviews, distribute VNRs/prepackaged news, and attempt to influence coverage and framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items 22–34 cover frequency of politician/official pressures, avoidance of topics that might offend politicians, leaks/off-the-record interviews (item 25), receipt and use of VNRs from government (item 26) and whether stations use such information as story basis or adopt the angles provided (items 27–30).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Relations Influence and Use of VNRs / Prepackaged Materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations practitioners attempt to influence which stories are covered, how they are covered (angle/stance), and sometimes to prevent coverage; stations may receive and use PR materials and VNRs to spark stories or run with little editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey covers how often stations use PR materials as the basis for a story (item 35), frequency of PR influence on coverage and framing (items 36–38, 42–44), how often stations receive VNRs (item 39), use VNRs (item 40), and air VNRs with little to no editing (item 41). Distinguish VNRs from government vs. non-government sources (item 39 note).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic / Bottom-Line Pressures Compromising News Content
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceptions that television news content is compromised because of economic pressures, including pressures to avoid stories damaging to the organization's economic interests or to specially handle stories involving economically powerful companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured by items asking how often content is compromised by economic pressures (item 45), how often journalists are pressured to avoid covering certain stories for economic reasons (item 46), and how often journalists are pressured to handle stories involving companies with economic clout in a special way (item 47). These relate to items about profit-over-quality (item 5) and bottom-line pressures (item 6).

rubrics_metrics.name: IOMC Model Structure and Linear Process Hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The Interorganizational Model of Content (IOMC) posits a generally linear process from Extramedia to Organizational to Within-Media to Influence/Outcome on Content, though Organizational influences also can directly affect content without passing through within-media gatekeepers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The validated model showed mostly simple, non-divergent paths among constructs (see Figure 4.5 as referenced). Future research should test whether these linear relationships hold across contexts and whether reciprocal/bilateral influences exist between levels (e.g., Organizational influencing Extramedia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal / Bilateral Influence Possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Influences across levels (e.g., organizational and extramedia) may be bilateral rather than strictly unidirectional; examples include media owners contributing to political campaigns to secure favors, and politicians offering support in return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The discussion suggests future research should examine whether Organizational Influences can affect Extramedia Influences (e.g., owners' political contributions shaping political actors' responsiveness). This is a caution against assuming strict uni-directionality in modeling influence flows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) strengths and limits as evaluation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: SEM can (1) assess or correct for measurement error; (2) incorporate both observed and latent (factor) variables measured by observed indicators; and (3) model correlated errors, interrelations, and interactions/mediation effects. SEM is an a priori approach (hypotheses specified beforehand) and useful for theory testing, but it cannot necessarily establish true cause and effect because it is based on correlational data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SEM when hypotheses/theory guide model specification. Be aware SEM's advantages over conventional approaches (combines regression, path analysis, CFA) and its limitation in establishing causality. The study used SEM with a model-building approach requiring a large sample and data-splitting (explore/modify then confirm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Web Survey Methodological Advantages and Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Web surveys provide quick responses, may offer greater privacy than phone surveys, and are convenient for busy television journalists; however, they produce cross-sectional snapshots and carry sampling/response limitations (e.g., overrepresentation of larger-market reporters, required response rates for sufficient cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages listed: fast responses, privacy (can be taken on any computer), likely candid responses from reporters (further removed from business side, transient profession). Disadvantages: cross-sectional design only captures a single time point (longitudinal data recommended), potential sample bias toward larger markets because of response-rate and sampling constraints, and need to plan for sufficient response rate (e.g., 30%) to achieve necessary sample size for SEM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey administration, confidentiality, and IRB considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation is voluntary and confidential; names/contact used only for tracking responses and reminders; IRB approval information and contacts provided; survey estimated to take ~13 minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent text states privacy protections, who will have access to data, avoidance of deductive disclosure by limiting analyses to aggregate data, and IRB contact details (study number 07-0088). Recruitment messages emphasize voluntariness, confidentiality, and offer summary of findings on request.
